e.t: This word means “unclean,” describing something regarded as impure or unsuitable for what is holy. In the Greek New Testament, it is used as an adjective, especially in expressions involving unclean spirits. It can describe spiritual impurity and, depending on the surrounding passage, other conditions understood as making a person or thing unclean. The word occurs 32 times in the Greek New Testament, across 30 verses, from Matthew through Revelation. Its exact force in any particular verse is determined by the surrounding context.

e.t: This word means “to look for” or “to search.” It describes actively trying to find someone or something, rather than merely noticing it. In the Greek New Testament, it appears three times, each in a passage involving a deliberate effort to find someone. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains an intentional search or attempt to locate what is missing or sought.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to open,” “opens,” or “opened.” It describes the action of making something no longer closed, or the state of something becoming accessible. Depending on the sentence, it can refer to a person opening something, something being opened, or an opening that has occurred. The word appears 77 times in the Greek New Testament, so its basic sense is used across many kinds of passages, while the surrounding context identifies what is opened.

This Greek New Testament word describes someone as “stupid” or “uninstructed”—a person lacking sound understanding or proper instruction. The two meanings overlap in portraying someone who has not learned or does not judge wisely. It functions as a description of a person’s condition, not as a personal name or title. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Timothy 2:23; the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its specific force there.

The word means “acceptance.” It expresses the idea that something is received favorably or regarded as worthy of approval. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Timothy, where its repeated rendering is “acceptance.” Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains the receiving or approving of something. This word is therefore focused on acceptance itself, not on a person, place, or physical object.

e.t: This word means “be perplexed” or “to be puzzled”—to face something difficult to understand or decide. It describes a person who is uncertain, confused, or at a loss about what something means or what should be done. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, including descriptions of people who are perplexed in different situations. The central idea is not merely lack of information, but mental uncertainty when circumstances or questions seem difficult to resolve.

This word refers to a meal, especially an early meal of the day. It names an ordinary time of eating rather than a special religious act or spiritual experience. In the Greek New Testament, it appears three times, in Matthew and Luke, and its meaning remains centered on the meal itself. The surrounding passage determines what social setting or purpose the meal has in each verse, but the word’s basic sense is simply food eaten as a meal, commonly understood as an early meal.

This word refers to an enclosed area, especially a courtyard, palace compound, or sheepfold. Its central idea is a bounded place within or around a larger building or enclosure, rather than an open area. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 12 times, including uses rendered “palace,” “courtyard,” and “sheepfold.” The precise English choice depends on what kind of enclosed place the surrounding passage describes.

e.t: This Greek word points to a person or thing as “he,” “she,” or “it,” and can also express “him,” “her,” “his,” “its,” or “myself.” Its exact English wording depends on how it functions in the sentence, including whether it refers back to someone already mentioned or marks possession. It is extremely common in the Greek New Testament, occurring 5,594 times, so it serves several ordinary pronoun roles rather than carrying one fixed English translation.

This word means a bundle or bundles—things gathered and tied together as one group. It is a noun describing a collected group rather than a single item. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 13:30, and the English rendering there is “bundles.” The word’s precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is a tied or gathered bundle. This word refers to a language—the recognizable speech used by people from a particular place or group. In Acts, it appears six times, especially in scenes where people hear or address others in their own language. Its sense concerns spoken communication and the language being used, rather than a private thought or inward feeling. The word occurs only in Acts within the Greek New Testament, so its normal biblical use is seen there in references to language as something heard, understood, or spoken.

This word describes someone or something as just, right, or righteous—consistent with what is good and fair. It can identify a person recognized as upright, or describe conduct that accords with justice. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 79 times, showing that this is a well-established way of describing people and actions in relation to what is right. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to expel” or “to take out”—to cause someone or something to leave a place or position. It can describe removal in a straightforward sense, but its exact force depends on what is being expelled or taken out in the sentence. The word occurs 81 times in the Greek New Testament, so it covers repeated language of removal across the New Testament rather than a single specialized use. Its meaning remains centered on sending out, driving out, or removing.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to breathe into” or “to breathe on.” It describes directing breath toward or into something, rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at John 20:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a deliberate breathing action. The paired meanings emphasize breath as the central action expressed by the word.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to praise”: to speak well of someone or recognize that person’s good qualities or actions. It functions as a verb, describing the act of giving approval or commendation. It occurs six times in five New Testament verses, including passages in Luke, Romans, and 1 Corinthians. Its use can refer to praising people for conduct that deserves approval, while the surrounding verse determines exactly who is being praised and why. The central idea remains an expressed commendation or favorable acknowledgment.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word is an adverb meaning “extremely” or “finally.” It intensifies a description by expressing the highest degree, or it can point to something happening at the very end. In the Greek New Testament it occurs once, in Mark 5:23. Which sense is intended depends on the sentence and surrounding passage, but the word itself adds the idea of extremity or finality rather than naming a person, object, or action.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “readily.” It is an adverb, so it describes how an action is carried out rather than naming a person, thing, or action itself. It marks an action as being done readily. The word appears three times in the Greek New Testament, in Acts, 2 Corinthians, and 1 Peter. Its exact force in any one verse is determined by the surrounding sentence.

This word means “weed,” referring to an unwanted plant growing among cultivated grain. It is used eight times in the Greek New Testament, all in Matthew 13, where the repeated term describes the plants found among the wheat in the parable and its explanation. The word therefore identifies a plant that resembles or grows alongside the desired crop, but is distinguished from the wheat. Its precise significance in any individual occurrence depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is a weed among grain.

This word refers to drops—small portions of liquid that fall or appear separately. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 22:44, and its recorded rendering is “drops.” The word itself identifies the visible liquid portions, while the surrounding verse supplies what those drops are and why they matter. Its basic meaning is therefore simple and concrete: individual drops rather than a stream, pool, or large quantity. The exact significance in Luke depends on the verse’s full context, which is handled separately. This word means “cheerful,” describing a willing, glad spirit rather than a reluctant or sorrowful one. It is used once in the Greek New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 9:7, and functions as a descriptive word. Its basic sense points to an attitude marked by genuine gladness. The surrounding verse is needed to explain its particular force there, but the word itself expresses cheerfulness plainly.

Iturea is the name of a region or territory. As a proper place name, it identifies a geographic area rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, the word occurs once, in Luke 3:1. The word itself supplies the place name, while the surrounding verse and passage provide the historical setting and explain how it functions there. Its meaning is therefore straightforward: Iturea refers to a particular region known by that name.

This word describes someone or something slanderous—speech or behavior that harms another person’s name through damaging accusations. It functions as a description of people characterized by this kind of speech. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Romans 1:30, so its broader scriptural use cannot be traced through multiple passages. Its central meaning remains clear: being slanderous, or marked by injurious speech against others.

Lasea is a name referring to a specific location in the Greek New Testament. The word is not a general description of an action, quality, or object; it identifies something by name. It appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 27:8. Its precise setting and significance come from the surrounding passage, but the word itself simply names Lasea rather than expressing an idea or action.

This word means “legion” or “legions,” referring to a large, organized body rather than a single individual. It appears four times in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Its repeated use in these accounts preserves the idea of a considerable multitude or collective unit. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central meaning remains a legion: many gathered together as one group.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to cause sorrow” or “to grieve.” It describes bringing about sadness or experiencing deep sorrow, depending on how it functions in a sentence. The word appears 26 times in the Greek New Testament, across 21 verses, showing that it is used for sorrow in several settings rather than for one narrow kind of grief. Its central idea remains emotional pain or distress connected with loss, disappointment, or troubling circumstances. The surrounding passage is needed to determine who is grieving and what caused the sorrow in a particular verse.

e.t: “Not yet” indicates that something has not happened or does not presently hold, while leaving open the possibility that it may happen later. It is a time-related negative expression, marking a situation as unfinished or still pending rather than permanently impossible. This Greek New Testament word occurs twice, in Romans 9:11 and Hebrews 9:8, and its central sense remains “not yet” in both occurrences.

This word describes someone who is sober and temperate—clear-minded, self-controlled, and not ruled by excess. It is used of people whose conduct should show steady judgment and restraint. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in instructions concerning church overseers, women, and older men. The word therefore points to a settled quality of character that helps a person act wisely and responsibly rather than impulsively or indulgently.

This word means a hindrance or impediment—something that gets in the way and makes progress more difficult. It is a noun describing an obstacle that must be set aside or removed rather than a person or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 12:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a burdening obstacle that interferes with forward movement.

This word means “hole,” referring to an opening or hollow space. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Hebrews 11:38 and once in James 3:11. Its basic meaning is straightforward, but the exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context. The word is therefore a concrete noun describing a physical opening rather than an action, quality, or person.

e.t: This word means to adjure or command, expressing a forceful charge that calls upon someone to comply. It describes more than a casual request: the speaker places the other person under a solemn demand. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only twice, in Mark 5:7 and Acts 19:13. Its exact force in either passage is clarified by the surrounding words, but its central sense remains a serious command or adjuration directed toward another person.

e.t: This word means “when”. It marks the time at which something happens, helping connect one event or statement with another. It can introduce a particular moment, period, or circumstance in the flow of a sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it appears 103 times, showing that this is a common time-related word rather than a term limited to one setting. Its meaning remains centered on identifying timing, while the surrounding words show what happened at that time. It occurs throughout the New Testament, from Matthew through Revelation.

This Greek New Testament word means “level,” describing something even or flat rather than raised or uneven. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Luke 6:17. As a lexical term, it functions as a straightforward description of a level place or surface. The surrounding verse is needed to explain precisely what it describes there; the word itself supplies the basic idea of evenness or flatness.

e.t: This word means to buckle a belt around oneself or to gird, describing the act of securing clothing with a belt. In the New Testament, it refers to being dressed or fastened in this way, and can describe something worn around the body. Its basic picture is practical: gathering clothing and fastening it so a person is ready to move or serve. It occurs six times in the Greek New Testament, in passages from Luke, Ephesians, and Revelation.

Pilate is the personal name of a person mentioned in the New Testament. It functions as a proper name rather than a description of a quality, action, or object. The name occurs 55 times across 53 New Testament verses, appearing most often in John, Luke, Mark, and Matthew. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies Pilate.

This Greek New Testament word means “somewhere” or “where?” and points to a place or asks about a location. It functions as a location word, directing attention toward the place connected with a person, thing, or action. It occurs 48 times in the Greek New Testament, across 43 verses, so it is a recurring way Scripture identifies or asks about place. Its precise force in a sentence may be either an actual question or a reference to an unspecified location.

This word means “before.” It marks something as occurring earlier, standing ahead, or coming prior to something else. It can describe order or position, depending on the sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 47 times, showing that it is a regularly used word for expressing what comes first or is placed in front. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains being before another person, thing, or event.

This word refers to an excuse or pretense—a stated reason or outward claim that can conceal a person’s real motive. It may describe presenting something as a justification when it does not honestly represent what is happening. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, showing this idea in several settings without changing its central sense. The surrounding verse determines whether the word emphasizes a false appearance, a claimed reason, or a motive hidden behind public words.

Ruth is a personal name referring to Ruth. In the Greek New Testament, this name occurs once, in Matthew 1:5. The word itself identifies a particular woman rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. Its meaning is therefore the person’s name, and understanding the significance of her mention requires the surrounding biblical passage. The name is rendered “Ruth” in the available English translations.

e.t: This word means to be devout or to worship, describing reverence directed toward God. It can refer to honoring God in worship or to a person characterized by sincere religious devotion. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 10 times, including passages where people are described as devout and passages that speak of worship. Its precise emphasis in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word means “wise” and can refer to people recognized for wisdom or understanding. In a sentence, it may describe the wise or address something as belonging to, being given to, or being directed toward the wise. It appears 20 times in the Greek New Testament, including uses in the Gospels, Romans, 1 Corinthians, Ephesians, and James. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Sychar is a proper name, referring to a place mentioned in the Greek New Testament. It is not a descriptive word or an action; it identifies a specific location. The name occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in John 4:5, and is rendered “Sychar.” Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its larger context, but the word itself functions simply as the name of that place.

This word means “order” or “turn,” referring to an arranged sequence in which people or things have their proper place. It describes the idea that events happen in an appointed order rather than all at once or without arrangement. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 15:23. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is sequence, arrangement, or one person's turn following another.

This word means “such,” “such as these,” or “such as this.” It points to a person, thing, or situation as belonging to a particular kind already mentioned or understood. In a sentence, it identifies something by comparison or description rather than naming it independently. The word appears 57 times in the Greek New Testament, so its exact reference depends on the surrounding words and passage. It occurs from Matthew through 3 John, serving this pointing and describing function throughout the New Testament.

This word refers to relations—the connections or dealings people have with one another. It names the relational aspect of an interaction rather than describing a person, place, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Romans 1:26–27. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains the existence or nature of relations between people.

e.t: This word means to deride or make fun of someone. It describes speech or behavior that treats another person with ridicule rather than respect. As a verb, it portrays the act of mocking, whether through words, tone, or conduct. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 2:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is clear: to ridicule someone openly or dismissively.
